description: We are making a route for Mars!
summary:
Mars: How to helps an astronaut walk safely on Mars, stay in contact with the base and never get lost, even when the radio drops.
On Mars there is no GPS and no compass, hills block the radio signal, and hazards such as landslides or solar storms appear without warning. Earth is too far away to help in time. Our solution has two parts that work together:
A live map app, built on real NASA and USGS data of Jezero Crater, where Perseverance landed. It finds the safest walking route, re-plans in about one second when a hazard appears, and leads the astronaut to terrain shelter during a solar storm. The base gets a control screen; the astronaut gets a simple screen with an arrow, the distance and voice alerts.
Ari, a robot companion that walks with the astronaut. When terrain blocks the signal, Ari moves to a spot that sees both the base and the astronaut and relays the signal. If all radio is lost, the astronaut’s position is still estimated from step sensors on the knee and hip, compared with the slope of the map.
We checked our map against Perseverance’s own measurements: map slope and the tilt the rover measured agree with a correlation of 0.79 over 708 points. The astronaut and the events are simulated; the terrain is real.
The working prototype is online at https://mars-how-to.onrender.com and the code is at https://github.com/etsaoul/mars-how-to.
details:
What it does

Mars: How to keeps an astronaut safe during a walk on Mars (an EVA, extravehicular activity). It combines a live map app with Ari, a robot companion, so that the base always knows where the astronaut is and the astronaut always knows the safe way, even when the radio drops.

How it works

  1. Real terrain. We load a NASA elevation map of Jezero Crater (20 m per pixel, NASA Mars Trek), the USGS geologic map SIM 3464 and THEMIS thermal inertia data. From the elevation we compute slope and roughness for every point.
  2. Safe route. Each type of ground gets a “cost” (steep, rough or sandy ground costs more), and slopes above 20° are forbidden for the astronaut. An A* search finds the safest route from the base, placed at Perseverance’s real landing site, to a real point Perseverance later reached.
  3. Live re-planning. When a hazard appears, for example a landslide, that area is blocked and a new route is found in about one second. During a solar particle event, the app finds the nearest place where the terrain hides most of the sky and guides the astronaut there.
  4. The radio triangle. Radio signals travel in a straight line, so we check line of sight over the real terrain, including the curvature of Mars, between the base, Ari and the astronaut. When a hill blocks the link, Ari tests positions around the astronaut and drives to one that can see both. Ari then relays the signal.
  5. Location without GPS. Mars has no GPS and no global magnetic field for a compass. The astronaut’s position comes from radio ranging (UWB chips, 10 cm precision, up to 290 m range). If all radio is lost, a particle filter keeps estimating the position from step sensors on the knee and hip (step counting and heading), comparing the slope the astronaut walks on with the map. When the signal returns, the position is corrected within seconds.
  6. Two screens. The base sees a control dashboard: map, route, positions, radio links, position uncertainty and alerts. The astronaut sees a simple HUD with an arrow, the distance and voice alerts, so their eyes stay on the ground.

Benefits and impact

  • The astronaut is never “lost”: the base knows their position even during a radio blackout.
  • Hazards are handled locally in seconds, without waiting minutes for Earth.
  • The astronaut’s interface is minimal, which suits a heavy suit and gloves.
  • The same idea works on Earth wherever GPS fails: caves, mines, deep canyons, search and rescue.

Our goal is to make longer and safer surface walks possible for future Artemis and Mars crews.

Validity

We validated our map against Perseverance’s own measurements. At 708 real rover stops, the slope from our map and the tilt the rover measured agree with a correlation of 0.79. Their average difference (3.4°) is used as the noise level in our terrain matching. Slope limits follow Apollo (<15°) and Artemis (<20°) practice. We are open about our limits: the astronaut, the robot and the events are simulated, and some engineering values (antenna heights, terrain cost factors) are our own assumptions, listed in the code.

Tools and technologies

  • Languages: Python (back end), HTML and JavaScript (screens).
  • Libraries: FastAPI and WebSocket (live updates every second), NumPy and SciPy (terrain analysis), rasterio and pyogrio (reading NASA/USGS GIS data), Matplotlib and Pillow (map layers), HTML Canvas (drawing), Web Speech API (voice).
  • Algorithms: A* path search, line-of-sight analysis, particle filter for localization.
  • Deployment: GitHub and Render (cloud). Each visitor gets their own mission.
  • Hardware: none built. The design assumes existing parts: UWB ranging chips (DW1000 class) and inertial step sensors on the knee and hip.
  • AI: we used an AI assistant to help write the code and the presentation. The ideas, design choices and testing were done by the team.

What makes it creative

Most map solutions are static. Ours moves: a robot that goes where the signal is, and turns the base, robot and astronaut into a communication and positioning triangle. We also use the terrain itself as a backup “GPS”: the slope under the astronaut’s feet, matched to the map, tells us where they are.

Factors we considered

  • Safety first: human slope limits, avoidance of rough and sandy ground, shelter during radiation events.
  • Realism: real NASA/USGS data, Mars curvature in line-of-sight checks, real sensor accuracy from datasheets, and a check against the real rover.
  • Honesty: every assumption is written in the code and on the dashboard. We say clearly what is real and what is simulated.
  • Ideas we tested and rejected: using radiation, gravity or weather to locate the astronaut. These change too little over short distances to help.
  • Usability: minimal information for the astronaut, full detail for the base.
